title: Downtown Guelph renewal: streetscape, waste and washrooms
subtitle: Also: Indigenous Relations Framework, heritage district, renter supports, and a letter opposing provincial bike lane limits.
overview: Council approved a package of measures for the Downtown Infrastructure Renewal Program. These include an enhanced streetscape with more trees, seating and paving stones, with a budget increase estimated at $17.1 million to be adopted through 2025 budget confirmation. Council also approved enhanced downtown waste collection, including communal underground containers, and a plan for more public washrooms, including a self-cleaning washroom at the Wyndham Street and St. George's Square redevelopment.

Council also approved the Indigenous Relations Framework and asked staff to prepare a plan and guidelines for a Downtown Guelph Heritage Conservation District. The consent report included a directive to create an eviction survey and a "Renting in Guelph" web page for renters.

Late in the meeting, council suspended its procedure by-law {{vote:m12}} so a councillor could bring forward a motion. Council then agreed {{vote:m13}} to have the mayor write to provincial leaders opposing reported plans to restrict municipal bike lane placement. After a closed session on a possible legal claim, the mayor reported only that council received information and gave direction to staff.

decisions.detail: Council approved enhanced streetscaping for downtown renewal, with a budget increase estimated at $17.1 million to be adopted through 2025 budget confirmation, and directed staff to prepare design and tender for Wyndham Street North construction with mitigation measures.

Council approved an enhanced level of waste collection service downtown, including public space containers and communal underground containers, with a project budget estimated at $1.0 million and an operating increase of $410,000 to be adopted through 2025 budget confirmation.

Council approved a set of measures to expand public washrooms, including underground infrastructure for self-cleaning washrooms in each downtown renewal phase, one at Wyndham Street and St. George's Square, continued portable washrooms, and exploring drinking water fountains.
Council approved the Indigenous Relations Framework for the City of Guelph.
Council approved the study's recommendations and directed staff to prepare a plan and guidelines for the Downtown Guelph Heritage Conservation District under the Ontario Heritage Act.
Council directed staff to create an eviction survey and a "Renting in Guelph" landing page to guide renters on their rights and resources.
Council approved the budget adjustments in Tables 4, 5 and 6 of the 2024 second quarter budget monitoring report.

decisions.item: Letter on provincial bike lane plans
decisions.detail: Council directed the mayor to write to provincial leaders and municipal associations opposing reported provincial legislation limiting municipal bike lane placement, and to request investment in public transportation instead.

debate: A cycling advocacy delegate supported the flexible downtown street design, trees and washrooms, but said bike connections into downtown are missing, and suggested a lower-slope route via Cardigan Street. Staff said the advocacy group would be consulted in the cycling and transportation master plan update and in detailed design.

One councillor asked what happens if the accessibility advisory committee objects to paving stones. Staff said they were surprised, since pavers can mark different areas, and that they would review the design with the committee in December.

A delegate who spoke on the Indigenous Relations Framework urged everyone to examine personal bias. A delegate on washrooms said access to washrooms and drinking water is limited downtown, especially in the evening.
A councillor asked about timelines for portable washrooms, park washrooms and drinking water access. Staff said initial discussions had happened and promised to follow up by email.

On the bike lane letter, supporters said the province often acts quickly after seeking input, so early comment could matter. The mayor opposed it because the legislation had not been tabled and said decisions should wait for that.
